```{r setup, include = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE,
                      purl = FALSE)
library(castSDM)
```

## Overview

`castSDM` explains environmental drivers and the spatial pattern of predicted
habitat change. Its central question is: where would suitability improve or
decline under an environmental change, and how does each driver contribute?

`cast_attribution()` compares paired current and future environments with one
fitted SDM and fixed ensemble weights. It returns overall change, driver-only
effects, retained-driver contrasts, training-range flags and model disagreement.
The same numerical implementation serves tables and aligned rasters.

When models are already fitted with a mature tool, use its prediction method
directly instead of repeating fitting in castSDM:

```{r external-model, purl = FALSE}
fit <- cast_as_fit(list(gam = fitted_gam), training_predictors,
  function(model, newdata) predict(model, newdata, type = "response"))
attribution <- cast_attribution(fit, current_predictors, future_predictors)
plot(attribution, contrast = "retained")
```

The training reference contains predictors in the original modelling units.
The callback owns preprocessing and returns one comparable suitability per row.
Use explicit externally validated weights for multiple models when needed;
the adapter does not create evaluation evidence. To evaluate internally fitted
models with an existing spatial design, supply its integer assignments through
`cast_cv(fold_ids = ..., k = ..., n_repeat = 1)`.

The existing fitting, selection and spatial-validation APIs remain available.
RF / BRT / MaxEnt / GAM engine packages perform fitting. This walkthrough uses
the standard pipeline to obtain a fitted model, then explains environmental
scenarios. When variable selection is used, re-run it inside validation folds.

## Data

Species data are presence/background tables with `lon`, `lat`, `presence`
(0/1) and environmental predictors. The following synthetic table demonstrates the API:

```{r data, purl = FALSE}
library(castSDM)

# Synthetic demonstration data; not an empirical case or validation result.
set.seed(1)
n <- 400L
dat <- data.frame(lon = runif(n, 90, 100), lat = runif(n, 25, 35),
  bio01 = rnorm(n, 12, 3), bio12 = runif(n, 300, 1200), elevation = runif(n, 500, 4000))
dat$presence <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis((dat$bio01 - 12) / 3 + (dat$bio12 - 700) / 400))

```

## One-step pipeline

`cast_run()` is the single production pipeline. It is driven by a
`cast_protocol()` -- the one place where every scientific setting is
declared -- and follows the four evaluation rules: selection, thresholds and
ensemble weights are estimated on the training split; the hold-out split is
evaluated exactly once with the out-of-fold thresholds; the published
predictions use the full-data refit; and the ensemble threshold comes from
the out-of-fold ensemble surface it is applied to.

```{r pipeline, purl = FALSE}
protocol <- cast_protocol(
  models = c("rf", "gam"),
  cv_k = 3,
  tune = FALSE,
  seed = 42
)
result <- cast_run(dat, env_data = dat, protocol = protocol, verbose = FALSE)

summary(result)
plot(result$screen)
print(result$protocol)
```

```{r eval, purl = FALSE}
result$eval$metrics       # one-shot hold-out evaluation (out-of-fold thresholds)
result$cv$thresholds      # per-engine thresholds pooled from out-of-fold predictions
```

## Environmental scenarios

Supply future values for every fitted predictor. Unchanged predictors stay at
their current values; do not manufacture future values for static layers.
This synthetic example changes one fitted predictor by one fifth of its SD.

```{r paired-scenarios, purl = FALSE}
future <- dat
driver <- result$fit$env_vars[1]
future[[driver]] <- dat[[driver]] + 0.2 * sd(dat[[driver]])
attribution <- cast_attribution(result$fit, dat, future,
                               cv = result$cv, method = "weighted",
                               verbose = FALSE)
attribution$summary
plot(attribution, contrast = "retained")
plot(attribution, type = "map", driver = driver)
```

The driver-only contrast changes that predictor while keeping all others
current. The retained-driver contrast compares the full future with a future
where that predictor stays current. They can differ when the response depends
on the other predictors. Individual effects need not add to overall change;
the remainder includes joint responses and changes in omitted drivers.

For rasters, supply stacks with identical grid geometry and CRS; `filename`
sets the output GeoTIFF. Raw scenario comparisons remain available outside
the marginal training ranges, with supported summaries reported separately.

## What each stage measured

`cast_importance()` shows the selection path from the screen: each admitted
predictor with its admission rank from the covsel embedding (1 =
strongest). There are no p-values and no count cap to read around.

```{r importance, purl = FALSE}
imp <- cast_importance(result$screen)
imp
plot(imp)
```

## Shift effect and masking

```{r attribution, purl = FALSE}
eff <- cast_effect_table(result$fit, newdata = dat, shift = 1,
                         verbose = FALSE)
eff        # rank supported drivers by mean_abs_dHSS; masked drivers read NA
plot(eff)  # cross = masked: the shift is not answerable inside the box

# The first-admitted driver is guaranteed to be fitted.
v1 <- result$screen$selected[1]
```

Give the shift in raw units whenever it has ecological meaning, for example
`shift = list(bio01 = 2)` for +2 degrees. A shift that leaves the training
range everywhere is refused rather than answered.

## Spatial prediction on a grid

```{r predict, purl = FALSE}
# Build a small prediction grid from the data range.
grid <- expand.grid(
  lon = seq(min(dat$lon), max(dat$lon), length.out = 20),
  lat = seq(min(dat$lat), max(dat$lat), length.out = 20)
)
env_vars <- result$fit$env_vars
for (v in env_vars) {
  grid[[v]] <- median(dat[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)
}

pred <- cast_predict(result$fit, grid)
plot(pred, basemap = "none")
```

## Interpretation

These maps explain the fitted model under stated environmental scenarios.
They do not establish which factor caused an observed distribution change.
Observation bias, correlated predictors and missing ecological processes can
affect the explanation. Future projection assumes the fitted response remains
applicable and does not model dispersal or colonisation.

On presence/background data the scale is relative suitability, not occurrence
probability. Training-range flags check each predictor separately; they do not
detect every unsupported joint combination. Cross-model SD reports disagreement,
not sampling uncertainty or a confidence interval. Single-shift products use
hard masking, whereas paired attribution retains raw contrasts and separately
reports their range coverage.
